title: Exodos (lines 1626–1831)

teacherSummary.text: A messenger reports Oedipus' last farewell and his mysterious passing, seen only by Theseus. The daughters mourn. Theseus keeps his promise not to reveal the grave and promises them his care. Antigone resolves to return to Thebes.

items.prompt: Does this ending show the cursed man becoming a protector of the city? Defend a reading from Theseus's kept charge and from the rest promised to the realm, without turning the hidden tomb into a puzzle to be solved on stage.
items.expected: Yes, in the form this play allows. Theseus reports that if he keeps the hest he shall hold his realm at rest, and he has pledged his word to Zeus; he then refuses to show the tomb and still promises the daughters his care. The protection is not a visible monument and not a public funeral. It is a secret kept by the king, offered as a defence of the land, after a painless passing that only he has seen. A careful reading can also note the limit: the daughters do not see the place, and they turn toward another city's feud. The protector's gift is the oath and the rest it is said to secure, not a grave the audience is invited to find.

The messenger says they saw him move hence, and they must know how: without a friend to lead the way, he himself was guiding them all. “How he moved hence, you saw him and must know; / Without a friend to lead the way, himself / Guiding us all.” (lines 1634–1636). The blind man leads the seeing, even at the last, to the abrupt earth-rooted threshold. The detail is not a claim that he has recovered ordinary sight. It shows that the summons still gives him a path, and that the others follow until the moment when only Theseus may stay.

He prays that Theseus be brought, and when the prince comes nearer he asks for a joined pledge: Theseus is to give his right hand, the daughters theirs, and Theseus is to promise never to forsake them, but to do all that time and friendship prompt. “Pledge ye my daughters, giving thy right hand— / And, daughters, give him yours—and promise me / Thou never wilt forsake them, but do all” (lines 1676–1678). The messenger adds that Theseus repressed his tears and swore to be their constant friend. The pledge is a charge of care for the living, given at the edge of the end, and it is not a request that anyone share his death.

Yes, in the form this play allows. Theseus reports that if he keeps the hest he shall hold his realm at rest, and he has pledged his word to Zeus; he then refuses to show the tomb and still promises the daughters his care. The protection is not a visible monument and not a public funeral. It is a secret kept by the king, offered as a defence of the land, after a painless passing that only he has seen. A careful reading can also note the limit: the daughters do not see the place, and they turn toward another city's feud. The protector's gift is the oath and the rest it is said to secure, not a grave the audience is invited to find.

Ismene says he died tombless, with none near; Antigone answers by asking to be led to that place and slain there (lines 1777–1778). Ismene then asks how she herself can drag on a friendless, helpless life. The chorus tells the maids not to fear, and says that refuge has been found, where they shall be safe from harm. “Fear not, maids—” (line 1782). “Refuge hath been found.” (line 1784). “Where thou shalt be safe from harm.” (line 1786). Theseus later dries their tears and promises his care.

“My children, ye will lose your sire today,

Have ye to bear your long, long ministry;

Wipes out all score of tribulations—love.

For the call came, now loud, now low, and oft.

Too long, too long thy passing is delayed.”

A messenger reports Oedipus' last farewell and his mysterious passing, seen only by Theseus. The daughters mourn. Theseus keeps his promise not to reveal the grave and promises them his care. Antigone resolves to return to Thebes.

items.text: What does the messenger say Theseus did with his hand, after the passing was complete?
items.lookFor: He shaded his eyes, as from some awful sight. The messenger places that gesture after the man was gone, a sign of what may not be told, and not a naming of the secret place itself.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He shaded his eyes, as from some awful sight. The messenger places that gesture after the man was gone, a sign of what may not be told, and not a naming of the secret place itself.

items.text: Why does Theseus keep the grave secret?
items.lookFor: He promised Oedipus; the secret protects Athens.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Theseus is bound by an oath: Oedipus “Charged me straitly that no mortal / Should approach the sacred portal” (lines 1812–1813), and “to Zeus I pledged my word” (line 1819). The secret is also the city’s protection: “If thou keep’st my hest / Thou shalt hold thy realm at rest” (lines 1816–1817). Keeping it is both loyalty to his friend and care for Athens, even though it means refusing the grieving daughters.

items.text: What does “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” suggest about the mysterious passing? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: The cursed man becomes a protector of the city, and his farewell to his daughters turns on the word “love” (line 1661).
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The Exodos suggests that the outcast’s end is a blessing, not a disgrace: “without wailing or disease or pain / He passed away—an end most marvellous” (lines 1704–1705), and his hidden grave will keep Athens “at rest” (line 1817). His farewell sums up his life with his daughters in one word: “one word / Wipes out all score of tribulations—love” (lines 1660–1661).

items.text: Find one example of plot in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”. What does it reveal about the mysterious passing that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A plot example, such as only Theseus seeing the end while the Messenger reports only what he did not see, explained for what it reveals: the mystery itself is the meaning.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The Messenger and the others look back and find that “The man was gone, evanished from our eyes” (line 1692), while Theseus shades his eyes “as from some awful sight” (line 1694). The plot keeps the moment itself offstage and unknown: “No man save Theseus knoweth” (line 1699). A plain statement that Oedipus died would miss how the play makes his end a holy mystery.

items.text: How does the theme in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” shape what we understand about the mysterious passing?
items.lookFor: How the theme of love outlasting suffering (“Love can turn past pain to bliss”) shapes the ending: grief is real, but the care the daughters gave is honoured.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The theme of love outlasting suffering frames the grief. Oedipus tells his daughters that one word “Wipes out all score of tribulations—love” (line 1661), and Antigone answers in her lament: “Love can turn past pain to bliss, / What seemed bitter now is sweet” (lines 1742–1743). The theme shows that the care they gave was not wasted, even in their sorrow.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “This promise given, Oedipus…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from lines 1682–1688 with their connotations, such as “Blind hands,” “nobility” or “Unlawful,” showing a last blessing and a holy limit the daughters must respect.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The phrase “Blind hands” (line 1683) makes his last touch both tender and helpless, a blessing given by a man who cannot see his children. Then he tells them to “prove your true nobility” (line 1684) by leaving, rather than by staying. The diction makes leaving an act of honour and marks the holy limit that even his children must not cross.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is the god’s call, which ends the farewell and sends everyone but Theseus away; its effect is to leave the daughters grieving without a grave and to put them in Theseus’s care.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is the voice that calls him: “Oedipus, Oedipus, why tarry we?” (line 1671). It ends the farewell and leads him to place his daughters in Theseus’s care, “Thou never wilt forsake them” (line 1678), before sending them away. The effect follows: the daughters are left without even a grave to visit, and Theseus must keep both his oath of secrecy and his promise to care for them.

items.text: How does “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” build on “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: the elders prayed for a gentle, tearless end, and the Messenger reports an end “without wailing or disease or pain,” as if the prayer was answered.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In Stasimon 4 the elders prayed that the stranger be sped “By a gentle, tearless doom” (line 1610). The Exodos answers: “without wailing or disease or pain / He passed away” (lines 1704–1705). The Chorus even asks, “By a god-sent, painless doom, poor soul?” (line 1632). The prayer seems answered, which makes the end feel like a blessing.

items.text: In “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the mysterious passing, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive behind words: Antigone claims to want only to see the grave, but her grief and her talk of going home show that she is looking for somewhere to belong; Theseus’s refusal comes with care.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Antigone asks, “With our own eyes we fain would see / Our father’s tomb” (lines 1807–1808). Her deeper motive shows in her other words: “How again to get us home / I know not” (lines 1789–1790). She is looking for something to hold on to now that her life of caring for him is over. Theseus refuses the request, but he promises to “on all your needs attend” (line 1828), answering the deeper need.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (How can grief and love be present at the same time?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (grief and love together), using Antigone’s lament or the farewell, where love and loss are spoken in the same breath.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said grief and love come one after the other. Antigone shows they can be the same feeling. She misses even the work of caring for him: “Ah me! that happy toil to miss, / The guidance of those dear blind feet” (lines 1744–1745). The toil was hard but happy because of love, and losing it hurts for the same reason.

items.text: Where does characterization appear in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”, and how does it connect the mysterious passing to the larger concern with guilt and intent?
items.lookFor: Where characterization connects the passing to guilt and intent: the man who called himself polluted ends honoured and painlessly taken, and the daughters’ lament names the curse they carry though they did nothing.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The man who once called himself “Corrupt and tainted” (line 1193) goes to his end calmly, blessing his daughters and his host, and is taken “without wailing or disease or pain” (line 1704). That supports his plea that he was guilty in deed but not in intent. Antigone still weeps “the curse that lay / On him our sire” (lines 1714–1715), so the play shows its burden passing to children who intended nothing.

items.text: Open question: is the ending happy, sad, or both? Defend any position.
items.lookFor: A defended position: both, with evidence for sorrow (the daughters’ grief, the feud ahead) and for peace (a painless end, a protected city, care for the daughters), and a counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: both. The end of Oedipus is peaceful, “an end most marvellous” (line 1705), and the Chorus calls it “blessèd” (line 1764). But the daughters are left grieving and homeless, and Antigone goes back to Thebes to try to “Heal this mortal feud” (line 1823). Counter-line: a reader could call it mainly hopeful, since Theseus promises to look after them (lines 1826–1829). A strong answer distinguishes the end of Oedipus from what his daughters face.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The cursed man becomes a protector of the city. His last word to his daughters is "love" (line 1661). How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines: the hidden grave makes him Athens’ protector and love sums up his farewell, with a correction that “love” is not literally his last word (he later blesses them and sends them away).
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: mostly agree, with a correction. He does become a protector: “If thou keep’st my hest / Thou shalt hold thy realm at rest” (lines 1816–1817). His farewell does turn on “love” (line 1661). But it is not literally his last word to his daughters: he later tells them to “prove your true nobility” and leave (lines 1684–1685). The claim is true in spirit, not in detail.

items.text: Which character in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” acts most wisely in the matter of the mysterious passing, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two characters, for example keeping faith under grief: Theseus keeps his oath and his promise to the daughters, while Antigone’s grief pushes her toward what is forbidden. With a line for each and care for her grief.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of keeping faith, Theseus acts most wisely: he keeps the secret, “to Zeus I pledged my word” (line 1819), and keeps his promise to the daughters, “nor will I spare / Aught of toil and zealous care” (lines 1826–1827). Antigone’s wish to see the grave (lines 1807–1808) goes against her father’s command, though it comes from love and grief, not folly. She acts wisely in the end when she yields, “We must yield” (line 1821), and turns to healing her brothers’ feud.

items.text: You are directing “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the mysterious passing.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the Messenger shielding his eyes as he describes Theseus, or Theseus kneeling to the daughters as he promises care, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) On “Only the king we saw with upraised hand / Shading his eyes” (lines 1693–1694), have the Messenger raise his own hand and look away, so the audience feels the awe without seeing anything. (2) On “Go in peace; nor will I spare / Aught of toil and zealous care” (lines 1826–1827), have Theseus kneel and take both daughters’ hands. The audience sees that the host’s promise to their father continues in his care for them.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1626–1831: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: What does Oedipus ask his daughters to fetch before the end? (Running water, to wash and make libation, lines 1644–1646.) Why/how: Why does Theseus shade his eyes? (He sees something “That no man might endure to look upon,” line 1695.) Should/what if: Should Theseus let the daughters see the grave? (Answers weigh their grief, lines 1807–1808, against his oath, lines 1812–1819.)

items.text: Connect “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)”, with its focus on the mysterious passing, to curse and mercy: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about curse and mercy, the question’s theme. The ending gives mercy to Oedipus and his daughters, but the curse on the brothers still stands; a strong answer says what remains unresolved.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong and deliberately unfinished. Oedipus receives mercy, a painless end and a grave that protects his hosts (lines 1704–1705), and Theseus promises his daughters mercy (lines 1826–1829). But the curse is not lifted: Antigone goes to try to “stay / The self-wrought doom / That drives our brothers to their tomb” (lines 1823–1825). The play leaves the brothers’ fate outside its ending, as if mercy could reach only so far.

items.text: Is the plot in “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” effective in presenting the mysterious passing, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (is reporting the end better than showing it?), with a line that meets the criterion and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because reporting keeps the mystery. We hear only that “The man was gone, evanished from our eyes” (line 1692), which keeps the end holy and beyond sight. Counter-line: the long lament and back-and-forth that follow (lines 1711–1800) may feel drawn out to some readers. A strong review weighs whether that length honours the grief or slows the end.

items.text: Compare how “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” treats the mysterious passing with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (another story whose hero’s end is hidden or reported, or whose grave is unknown) and one thing the Exodos sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare the death of Moses at the end of Deuteronomy (34:6), where no one knows the place of his grave. Both endings hide the grave. The Exodos adds a human cost the other story does not dwell on: the daughters who cared for him are refused even a visit, “That may not be” (line 1809). The play sees that a sacred secret can protect a city and still hurt the people who loved the dead.

items.text: As the final scene, does this ending resolve guilt and intent? Argue whether the ending is earned.
items.lookFor: A judgment on guilt and intent, the question’s theme: the ending supports Oedipus’s claim that his guilt lay in deed, not intent, by giving him a gentle, god-sent end, but the curse still weighs on his family. Is that ending earned?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the ending largely resolves guilt and intent for Oedipus himself. The man who said he acted “all unwitting” (line 265) is called by a god, “Oedipus, Oedipus, why tarry we?” (line 1671), and taken without pain (line 1704), which treats his innocence of intent as real. It is earned because the play argued the case from the Parodos onward. But it does not resolve everything: Antigone still names “the curse that lay / On him our sire” (lines 1714–1715), and the brothers’ feud remains (lines 1822–1825).

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the mysterious passing?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a once-rejected elder dies peacefully in a place that took him in, his resting place is kept secret, and his host promises to care for his grieving family. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: An old exile dies quietly in the town that took him in. Only the mayor knows where he is buried, because the old man asked for secrecy, and the mayor refuses even the daughters while promising to support them. Two things must stay: the hidden grave as a promise kept (lines 1812–1819), and the host’s care for the daughters after the death (lines 1826–1829).
